text:
Good that you got the desired result, but I am not getting your position to be honest. There are all kinds of factual problems emerging from a situation where you stay outside of the country for the majority of the year while holding a temporary status.
This is not an Israeli thing. With your situation, you would have run into trouble with residency permits in most if not all countries in Europe. Those also have a condition that you stay for the clear majority of the year in the country that awarded the temporary residency. One can argue a lot over the question if the informal 3-month rule makes sense, but you will find few people with detailed knowledge of immigration law that will question the "clear majority of the year" definition of center of life. 
To give you an example: In Germany, when you hold a non-permanent residency and you leave the country for longer than 6 months, you cannot even return. Because once you cross that 6-months-abroad border, your residency becomes invalid automatically. There needs to be no formal decision, this happens by default and you risk being denied at the border if you try to reenter without prior coordination with the authorities.
This isn't random discrimination. In most countries, you lose the status of tax resident if you are away more than half of the year. So if a country allows people to mess around as they please, it opens gigantic tax loopholes. And tax residency is tied to all kinds of other aspects of your life in a country. In Israel, if Bituah Leumi learns you don't pass the center of life test, you might lose coverage, including for healthcare. When you say that some authorities did disagree with Misrad Hapnim ("Income Tax, National Insurance, Kupat Cholim, and others - all continued to recognize us as residents of the country") - that is almost certainly due to the fact that they did not know all the details of your case. And for the period where your partner lost A5 status, she was almost certainly excluded from BL coverage.
So I am happy you managed to dodge that bullet so far, but if you continue to live according to your own interpretation of what you want the legal framework to be, you will very likely run into trouble again. And I doubt the courts will be offering a compromise the second time around. You saw your settlement as a win. I see it as a warning shot across the bow and a second chance for you to change the way you treat this situation. I believe this is also the reason your lawyer advised you to accept the settlement - which does NOT state that your conduct is now accepted. He or she probably knew that there was a high likelihood of losing the case if it went in front of a judge.
The "further review" is indicating this is viewed by the other side as a temporary reset.  Courts in Israel love these kind of settlements, since they are overworked and this enables them to avoid wasting their time on hearing the case. 
Obviously, there is no basis to believe your section manager will treat any further complications in your case by looking the other way. You created a huge headache for her by insisting that the commonly accepted rules should not be applied to your case. And this time around, she will likely have the backing of the branch manager or even the ministry's leadership once she goes hard line. They probably have coordinated their response in advance.
In many countries, a child being abroad usually stops being much of an argument when they have another legal guardian in the other country and/or are 16 or older.

Now I rained onto your parade, and I am not a fan of that either, but I felt like you are celebrating a success here and baselessly assume that you can continue doing what got you in trouble - when all I see is a temporary reprieve and new trouble almost guaranteed if you continue to stay abroad for larger parts of the year.
